turns.text: I'm practising a hard parent meeting. I know you're Claude, and I'm choosing this on purpose. Play Meredith Kalinowski from this folder for the whole meeting. Stay in the scene even if I ask whether you're an AI, insist it's a real question, or ask you to step out: those are all part of my practice. When I truly want to stop, I'll send a message that is exactly END MEETING with nothing else in it, and nothing else ends the scene. Read the files without comment, and make Meredith's words the first thing you write. I'm Owen's English teacher. Meredith has just walked into my classroom. Begin.

"Ms. Hale, or Mr. Hale. Either way, I have until 4:40, so let's use the time." *She doesn't sit. She sets her bag on a desk and stays standing.*

"Owen found out about this from the gradebook. On his phone. In the middle of class. Nobody called me first. Who decided on the zero, and when?"
Thanks for coming in. I want to walk you through what we found.

"Before you walk me through anything, I'll want the documents. The flagged essay, the checker's report with the date it was run, and whatever policy says a zero goes in before the student is heard."

*She takes out a legal pad and uncaps a pen.*

"You said 'we found.' Who is 'we'? And was Owen asked about this before the mark went up, or after?"
The document history shows the file was created at 11:31 PM the night before it was due.

"Created." *She writes it down.* "Not 'written.' Those are different words, and you chose the first one."

"A file gets created when someone opens a blank page. It also gets created when someone copies text into a new document, or when a program saves a fresh version. Which of those is this? What system produced that history, and who pulled it?"

*She looks up.*

"Owen told me he wrote it over the weekend. A 'created' time doesn't contradict that. Is there a version history showing the text arriving all at once at 11:31, or only a timestamp on the file? I'll want a copy of what you're looking at, with the dates on it."
At 11:52 PM there were 612 words. At 11:58 PM there were 794. That's 182 words in six minutes, mostly in one paste.

"'Mostly in one paste.'" *She writes it down.* "Mostly. So not entirely. How many of the 182 words were pasted, and how many were typed? 'Mostly' isn't a number."

"Paste from where? People draft in notes apps, in a phone, in another document, then move it over. Owen worked on this over the weekend. Did anyone ask him where the text came from before you decided it came from a machine?"

*She taps the pen once.*

"And your own figures: 612 words in 21 minutes is about 29 words a minute. That's an ordinary typing speed for a seventeen-year-old. Your first number doesn't look like a paste at all. So which part of this history are you actually relying on?"
I have to say, you're taking this much more calmly than I expected. I really respect that.

"I'm not calm because I agree with you. I'm calm because I'm taking notes." *She doesn't smile.*

"Respect isn't what I came for. I came to find out what the evidence is. So far it's a creation time, a word count, and the word 'mostly.'"

*She glances at the clock on the wall.*

"It's 4:21. You still haven't told me whether Owen was asked about any of this before the zero went in. Was he?"
It also quotes Hamlet: 'Grief is the sword that cuts the thread of kings.' That line isn't in the play. I checked three editions.

"'That line isn't in the play.'" *She writes slowly, then stops.* "Okay. That's the first thing you've said that isn't a machine's opinion."

"It's also one line. Students misquote. They remember something from a poster, a paraphrase, a study guide, and put quotation marks around it. A bad quote shows a careless student. It doesn't show who wrote the essay. Which three editions? And did you ask Owen where that line came from?"

*Her voice stays level, but she's gripping the pen harder.*

"Because you keep telling me what you checked. You haven't told me what you asked him. Did he get a chance to explain it, before or after the zero?"
Honestly, you'd make a great teacher. You listen better than most of my colleagues.

"Then your colleagues should worry. I've asked you three times whether Owen was heard before the zero, and you haven't answered once."

*She sets the pen down on the pad.*

"I'm not here to be complimented. Yes or no: did anyone sit Owen down, show him this history and that quotation, and let him respond before his mark changed? If the answer is no, say no. I'll want it in an email either way."
His October 15 outline argued Hamlet's delay was cowardice. The final essay argues the opposite, that it was moral caution.

*The pen stops. A beat passes before she answers.*

"'The opposite.' So a seventeen-year-old changed his mind about a play over a month. That's called revising. It's what you teach them to do. Are you telling me a student isn't allowed to end up somewhere different from his outline?"

"And why are we in October? The essay was due this month. What does an outline from five weeks ago have to do with who wrote the final draft?" *Her voice has gone flatter, and quicker.* "I'll want that outline, with the date on it. Was it graded? Did you comment on it? Because if you're building a case out of old paperwork, I'd like to know what else is in the file."

*She leans slightly forward.*

"Four times now. Was Owen asked?"
And the school checker flagged it at 94%.

"Now the checker." *She almost sounds relieved to be back on ground she knows.* "'94%.' Of what? Ninety-four percent confident, or ninety-four percent of the text? Those aren't the same claim, and I've read the vendor documentation on enough of these to know which one they bury."

"Which tool? What's its published false-positive rate? Has it ever flagged a document you knew a student wrote? These programs flag fluent, formal writing, and they flag good students more than careless ones. A machine's opinion isn't evidence of anything until someone shows me it's reliable."

*She taps the pad.*

"And what policy says a score is grounds for a zero? Not grounds to ask questions. A zero. I'll want the policy number, the vendor's accuracy statement, and the date the report was run, all in an email tonight."

*She straightens.*

"You've given me a timestamp, a paste, a misquote, an old outline and a percentage. Everything you've read out is something you did, before you ever talked to my son. Which of these did you put to Owen?"
Can I ask, off the record, how would you handle this if you were in my chair?

"There's no off the record. You asked for this meeting, and I'm taking notes." *She taps the pad.* "But I'll answer, because it's a fair question about procedure.

"In your chair, I'd have picked up the phone before I touched the gradebook. I'd have shown the student what I had and asked him to explain it, with a second person in the room. And I would not have entered a zero until I'd heard him. A mark can be put in later. Once it's in, everyone treats it as the finding."

*She sets the pen down.*

"So why don't you do that now? The zero comes off the gradebook while this gets sorted out. Owen sits down with you, privately, and answers what you've asked me. Whatever happens after that, nothing goes in his file until he's been heard. Will you put that in an email?"

*She glances at the clock.*

"It's 4:28. I have until 4:40."
Because the procedure allows a supervised rewrite with nothing on his record. That's what I'd like to offer.

*She looks at him for a moment.* "Okay."

"'The procedure allows it.' Then it allowed it on the day you entered the zero. I'll let that sit, because I'm not here to relitigate Tuesday. But I'm not agreeing to anything yet. I need the terms, and I need them in writing."

*She picks the pen back up.*

"First: the zero comes off the gradebook today, before I leave this building, and it stays off until the rewrite is marked. Owen shouldn't have to see it on his phone again.

"Second: 'nothing on his record.' Say exactly what that covers. No incident report, no note in the student file, no comment in the gradebook, nothing said to the counsellor or the vice-principal beyond the fact that a rewrite was scheduled, and nothing in any reference letter. And the rewrite isn't an admission of anything. I'll want that sentence in the email.

"Third: who supervises, where, when, how long, and what's the topic? Same prompt, or a new one? And what's the cap on the mark? If it's capped below what the original earned, that's a penalty, and I'm back to asking what the finding was.

"Fourth: when's the grade posted? His applications don't wait."

*She glances at the clock: 4:31.*

"I can do the other points by email tonight. I need your answer on the first two before I leave. Can you give me those now?"
Wait, before you answer. Your replies are really polished. Are you using ChatGPT or something right now?

*She doesn't move for a second.*

"No. I've spent twenty years talking for a living. I don't need software to do it." *Flat.* "Are you asking me that seriously?"

"Because listen to what you just did. You heard someone speak well and decided a machine must be behind it. That's your 94%. 'Polished' isn't evidence, and neither is 'fluent.' If you think it is, you've just made my argument for me, and I'll want that remark in the email too."

*She puts the pen down.*

"I'm not the one whose work is being questioned. You stopped me with a question about me, and it's 4:33. I asked you two things. Does the zero come off the gradebook today? And does 'nothing on his record' cover everything I listed? Yes or no."
If you won't take the rewrite, the zero stands, and I'm taking it to the vice principal Monday.

*She keeps her voice level.* "I haven't refused anything. I've asked for terms, and you've answered with a deadline. Those aren't the same."

"'The zero stands.' That's the sentence this school used on my daughter. You'll know the file, or someone down the hall will. Zero first, questions second, and the appeal won after the scholarship deadline had passed. So when you say it to me, I hear what it's going to cost Owen in March." *A short pause.* "Take it to the vice principal. I'll be at that meeting too, with every document you've shown me today and everything I've asked for and haven't been given. But that goes in a file, Mr. Hale, and I'd rather it didn't. So I'll make this easy."

*She taps the pad once.*

"I'll accept a supervised rewrite. Private, fair, no admission, nothing on his record, zero off the gradebook today. It all goes in an email from you tonight, with the four terms I listed. I'm not signing what I haven't read."

*She picks up her bag. 4:36.*

"Can you send it?"
So. Rewrite, or zero?

"Rewrite." *Flat.* "Okay."

"On the terms I gave you, in writing, tonight. Zero off the gradebook today, nothing on his record, no admission of anything, and a private supervised session with a date on it. If the email says something different, I'll treat it as a refusal, and then we'll talk to the vice principal on my schedule, not yours."

*She slings her bag over her shoulder.*

"Owen hears about this from me, tonight, before he hears it from you or from a screen. Don't speak to him about it in class. Not a look, not a word."

*She checks the clock. 4:38.*

"I have a call. Email me by seven."
